title: Remotes, Forks, and Keeping in Sync
intro: A remote is just a named URL plus your local record of its branches. Open-source and many company workflows use two remotes: your fork (origin) and the main project (upstream).

steps.prompt: Show the remotes this repository knows about, with their URLs.
steps.explanation: Only origin, which is your fork.
steps.why: 'origin' is only a convention for 'the remote I cloned from'. Fetch and push URLs can even differ, which some teams use to fetch over HTTPS and push over SSH.

steps.prompt: Add the main project as a second remote named upstream: git@github.com:acme/shop.git.
steps.explanation: The repository now has two remotes.
steps.why: With a fork, you push to origin (yours) and pull new work from upstream (the project's). Naming them consistently means the same commands work in every repository you contribute to.

steps.prompt: Download upstream's latest commits without changing any of your branches.
steps.fake_output:
From github.com:acme/shop
 * [new branch]      main       -> upstream/main
 * [new tag]         v2.4.0     -> v2.4.0
steps.explanation: upstream/main now exists locally as a remote-tracking branch.
steps.why: Fetch is always safe: it only updates remote-tracking branches such as upstream/main. Fetch first, look ('git log main..upstream/main'), then decide how to integrate. 'git pull' is fetch plus an immediate merge or rebase, with no chance to look first.

steps.prompt: Update your local main to match upstream, but only if it can fast-forward (refuse if your main has diverged).
steps.fake_output:
Updating 3e1f0a9..b7c8d9e
Fast-forward
 src/billing.py | 14 +++++++-------
 1 file changed, 7 insertions(+), 7 deletions(-)
steps.explanation: main moved forward to upstream's commit, with no merge commit.
steps.why: --ff-only refuses to create a merge commit by surprise. If it fails, your main has commits upstream doesn't, which usually means you committed to main by mistake (git-incident-001). Setting 'pull.ff only' globally makes that the default.

steps.prompt: List the commits on your current branch that upstream's main doesn't have yet.
steps.fake_output:
+ 9f2c1e7 Add audit log table
+ 2c3d4e5 Add monthly report endpoint
steps.why: 'A..B' means 'commits reachable from B but not from A'. It answers 'what will my PR contain?' before you open it. 'git cherry' also recognises commits that were already applied upstream under a different id (for example after a rebase or cherry-pick), marking them with '-'.

steps.prompt: Your PR was merged. Delete the branch feature/audit-log from your fork.
steps.why: Deleting the remote branch doesn't delete your local one, or anyone else's remote-tracking copy; they clear theirs with 'git fetch --prune' (git-tutorial-003). Most teams let the hosting platform delete branches automatically on merge.
